prompt: Show me how stochastic gradient descent works. Let me change the learning rate and batch size to see what happens.
refinement: Keep this simple: limit each run to 40 steps. Show at most 40 trail points for the current run and at most 40 for the saved comparison path. Keep the learning-rate and batch-size controls, the numerical readouts and the diverged state. Do not add a data panel, data points or any other new objects; the batch noise may be simulated, as long as the assumptions say so. Do not state numeric thresholds such as a stability limit unless they follow exactly from the stated formula. Do not add anything new.

plan.title: Stochastic Gradient Descent on a Loss Bowl: Learning Rate and Batch Size
plan.description: A 3D bowl-shaped surface shows the error (loss) for every pair of the two model settings, a slope w and an intercept b. A marker starts on the side of the bowl. Each step, it moves downhill along a noisy gradient (the direction of steepest uphill slope, which it steps against) and leaves a path of up to 40 points. Change the learning rate to see steps that crawl, zig-zag or blow up. Change the batch size to see a jittery path turn smooth.
plan.reason: You asked to change the learning rate and batch size. In an experiment you can change both and watch the path, the arrows and the numbers respond together, one step at a time.
interactions: Learning rate: small values creep, middle values reach the bottom fast, larger ones zig-zag across the steep direction, and past a certain size the run grows outward and stops as 'diverged'.
Batch size: with 1 point per step the path jitters and wanders near the bottom; bigger batches smooth it; at 64 the noise is exactly zero, so the path is smooth and the same every time.
Show or hide the grey full-data gradient arrow. Compare it with the step arrow, which shows the step actually taken, to see how far the noisy estimate is from the true direction.
Drag the start marker to a new spot on the bowl before you run.
Take one step: moves the marker by a single update so you can study it.
Use the card's step and pause controls to let the run continue (up to 40 steps) or to stop it.
New run, keep old path: starts again from the start marker with your current settings. The previous path stays in grey (up to 40 points) so you can compare.
assumptions: Simplified simulation: an idealized loss bowl with simulated batch noise, not a model trained on real data.
The loss is an exact bowl (a quadratic) with one lowest point. It is steeper along the intercept than along the slope.

Batch noise is simulated, not drawn from actual data points. Each step adds a random error to the exact gradient. Its spread is scaled the way it would be when sampling that many of 64 points without replacement, so it shrinks as the batch grows and is exactly zero at 64.
The update is: new settings = old settings − learning rate × noisy gradient.
The step arrow shows the step actually taken: minus the learning rate times the noisy gradient. The grey arrow shows minus the exact full-data gradient at the same spot, at the same scale.
Readouts: step number (out of 40), passes through the data (steps × batch size ÷ 64), full-data loss, and distance from the lowest point.
A run stops after 40 steps, or earlier as 'diverged' if the marker leaves the plotted area. The current path keeps at most 40 points, and so does the saved grey path.
Reset brings back the default settings and start point, clears both paths, and replays the same random noise from the fixed seed.
limitations: There is no real data, so the scene does not show data points, a fitted line or a real batch loss. The earlier batch-loss readout has been removed, and the noise is simulated.
A noisy step does not always lower the full-data loss. With small batches, single steps can go uphill. The loss falls only on average.
A bowl with a single lowest point cannot show the local minima, saddle points or flat regions found in deep-learning loss surfaces.
With small batches, unlucky noise can make a run diverge at a slightly smaller learning rate than with the full batch, or settle later.
The learning rate stays fixed, with no momentum, schedules or optimizers like Adam, so only your two settings change what happens.
plan.learningGoal: See that the learning rate sets the step size (too small is slow, too large overshoots or diverges), and that the batch size sets how noisy each gradient estimate is: small batches give jittery paths that wander near the bottom, and the full batch gives a smooth one.

authorDraft.title: Stochastic Gradient Descent on a Loss Bowl: Learning Rate and Batch Size
authorDraft.description: A bowl of stacked translucent blue rings shows the loss over slope w (left-right axis) and intercept b (front-back axis). The lowest point is marked at the centre. An orange ball starts on a green start puck and steps downhill. An orange arrow shows the next step it will take and a grey arrow shows minus the full-data gradient at the same scale. Orange dots trace the current path and grey dots a saved earlier path. A status label reads Ready, Running, Done or Diverged.
assumptions: Simplified simulation: an idealized loss bowl with simulated batch noise, not a model trained on real data.

Loss L = 0.5(0.5 w² + 2 b²), lowest at w=b=0, steeper along b. Update: new = old − learning rate × noisy gradient. With the full batch, b zig-zags above learning rate 0.5 and diverges above 1.0 (=2/2); the run stops as Diverged when |w|>4 or |b|>2.

Noise per component = 1.2 × N(0,1) × sqrt((64−B)/(63B)), the shrink factor for sampling B of 64 points without replacement: 1.2 at B=1 and exactly 0 at B=64. A noisy step can raise the full-data loss; it falls only on average.

The orange arrow is the next step at true scale (its tip is where the ball goes); the grey arrow is −learning rate × exact gradient at the same scale. Both are drawn at least 0.3 long for visibility, and the ball is enlarged.

While the card plays, one update happens every 8 host steps (about 0.27 s), up to 40. Changing learning rate or batch size restarts the current run from the start marker with the same noise, and keeps the saved grey path.
Dragging the start marker moves it along w only (b stays 1.3) and restarts the current run. Passes through the data (steps × batch ÷ 64) are left out to keep three readouts.
Reset restores default settings and start point, clears both paths and replays the same noise from the fixed seed. New run, keep old path draws new noise.

findings.message: The loss bowl is drawn as four flat translucent discs stacked at contour heights, not as a surface. The ball and path lie inside this stack, so the learner cannot see a downhill slope they ride on. Draw a real bowl (a quadratic mesh or wireframe) with the ball and dots sitting on it.

The current path is shown through 2–3 translucent disc layers, so the 'orange' dots and the orange ball look grey. They cannot be told apart from the saved grey path, which breaks the 'New run, keep old path' comparison. The current path needs to be drawn clearly orange, above the surface.

The gradient toggle is on and the run is going, but neither the orange step arrow nor the grey full-data gradient arrow can be seen at the bottom of the bowl. They are hidden under the discs and the ball. The noisy-versus-true comparison the plan promises cannot be read.
The plan's 'passes through the data' readout (steps × batch ÷ 64) is missing. The assumptions disclose this. Without it, small and large batches cannot be compared on equal data cost.
The middle learning-rate zig-zag regime (above 0.5) and the 'New run, keep old path' action were not sampled. The plan's 'drag to a new spot on the bowl' is limited to the w axis only.
At the low learning rate, the step arrow is a tiny stub next to the ball and is barely visible. Make it a thicker arrow that can be clearly seen.
The bowl is drawn as flat stacked discs rather than a surface, so the slope the ball creeps down cannot be seen.

After diverging, the program clamps the drawn position to |b|≤2. The ball is drawn at about distance 2.1 from the lowest point while the readout says 5.247 (b = −5.2). The picture disagrees with the readout, and the clamping is not disclosed. Show the real overshoot, or mark the ball as off-plot.
The diverged ball floats in empty space beyond the disc rim. No surface or path dot connects it to the start, so the outward blow-up cannot be read as a step.
From the side view, the path dots and ball are buried inside the stacked translucent discs and look grey. Neither arrow can be seen.
The step arrow cannot be seen. The ball overlaps the start puck.
The clamped diverged ball floats outside the bowl. Its drawn position disagrees with the readout distance of 5.247.

The plan promises a 'passes through the data (steps × batch size ÷ 64)' readout. The artifact only has loss, distance and step, so there is no number showing how much data each batch size uses for the same number of steps.

The plan promises a 3D bowl-shaped surface, but the loss bowl is drawn as four hairline contour rings and two hairline cross-sections. Nothing shows a shaded surface, so the bowl reads as loose ellipses and the ball and dots seem to float rather than sit on the loss surface.

Near the minimum, both arrows are forced to the 0.5 minimum length at 3× thickness. They become a stubby grey-and-red clump on top of the ball, the lowest-point marker and its label, so the learner cannot compare the noisy step with the full-data gradient direction, which the plan says this arrow pair is for.
The plan says the start marker can be dragged to a new spot on the bowl. It only drags along w, with b fixed at 1.3. This is disclosed in the assumptions.
Not sampled: the initial Ready state, 'New run, keep old path' (grey path), dragging, and middle learning rates where b zig-zags (0.5 to 1.0).
The 'passes through the data' readout promised by the plan is missing.

At learning rate 0.01 the real step is about 0.03, but the arrow is drawn at the 0.5 minimum length. It looks as large as an arrow at much higher rates, which hides the step-size effect, and it contradicts 'next step at true length'.
The bowl surface is drawn only as hairline rings, so the learner gets no sense of a surface the ball is creeping down.
